item.title: [LU-20276] sanityn test_70b test_71b test_71c: OOM crash for osd-zfs with ZFS 2.4.0

status.description: The issue is open and ready for the assignee to start work on it.

comments.comment: +1 sanityn test_71c: https://testing.whamcloud.com/test_sets/336d79c3-ac4d-45cc-a9cb-d89cd5ddefd6

This crashed about 90x in the past four weeks, exclusively on ZFS.

It looks like the crash is in ofd_destroy() for the cases I checked, which is a bit surprising since I wouldn't expect destroy to be using a lot of memory. Lustre itself is only using 148MiB of 3GiB on the VM, but that does not include page cache or ARC.
+1 on master: https://testing.whamcloud.com/test_sets/f925fa5b-c83f-41ca-9c5d-eb4c157819ba

+13 OOM crashes in test_70b the past week:
https://testing.whamcloud.com/search?status%5B%5D=CRASH&test_set_script_id=570ba67a-4a46-11e0-a7f6-52540025f9af&sub_test_script_id=52c5a802-7bc4-11e2-8242-52540035b04c&start_date=2026-07-07&end_date=2026-07-13&source=sub_tests#redirect

It is always failing on the OSS node. The sanityn test_70b test itself does not create or delete many files, so it is confusing why it is hitting OOM. I suspect some kind of strange overflow/underflow in the size calculation, or possibly some bad interaction between osd-zfs and the new ZFS 2.4.0 code that is being run for the past few months.
+1 sanityn test_71a: https://testing.whamcloud.com/test_sets/b74e6860-579c-4f80-8ea0-7f46f4d5fb8e

+6 crashes of 70b, +6 of 71c in the past week

More on master:
70b https://testing.whamcloud.com/test_sets/293b42a8-a534-43e3-875e-fd99ed9bdd96
71c https://testing.whamcloud.com/test_sets/5c5d5001-4991-4b4b-8e03-9ec9c3066cc7

Here is some AI's analysis of this OOM crash issue:

test_70b and test_71c are NOT the actual trigger — they're just innocent bystanders. The real culprit is test_56b (which runs earlier in the same sanityn.sh suite). test_56b creates a (16TB × OSTCOUNT) sparse, 2000-overstriped file via llverdev, writing 4KB chunks every 1GB offset (partial mode). When this massive sparse file is destroyed at test exit via stack_trap "rm -f", the client sends destroy RPCs and moves on quickly, but on the OSS the destroy is processed inline on the ptlrpc service thread: osd_trans_stop() → osd_unlinked_list_emptify() → osd_unlinked_object_free() → dmu_free_long_range(). This dirties the entire indirect block tree for each OST object, generating massive unreclaimable slab allocations (dbuf_dirty_record_t, dmu_buf_impl_t, zio_buf_comb_*, zfs_btree_leaf_cache, etc.) that silently exhaust free memory on the ~4GB test VM.

A userspace process (NetworkManager) does an ordinary page fault, finds no free pages, and invokes the OOM killer after ZFS consumed it all.

Reducing llverdev size in test_56b for ZFS would prevent this OOM crash, but we still need a thorough fix.

emoly.liu, can you please push a patch that adds wait_delete_completed after rm -f in the stack_trap in sanityn.sh::test_56b. That might help that test wait for the unlink to clean up a bit, but I'm not sure if that will free up the memory usage. The test shouldn't need to flush memory explicitly on the OSS for it to work properly (that should be handled by ZFS itself), but at least it can wait for the TXG commit before moving on to the next tests. While it would seem like there is a big gap between test_56b and test_70b, it looks like this is only 4s (only test_60 and test_70a in between, 2s each), so the wait_delete_completed call may be enough to allow this to pass consistently.

I don't think the llverdev file size should be reduced. The whole point of that subtest is to test a very large file (at the limits of ldiskfs, but it also shouldn't cause ZFS to fail).

behlendorf any chance you could look into the ZFS side of this? It seems like a mistake for ZFS to dirty so many unrelated indirect blocks and then consume all the RAM. There should be some kind of TXG flush and memory reclaim if the memory is getting low. We are seeing very regular OOM crashes with ZFS testing since the upgrade to ZFS 2.4 and it seems that this is one of the causes.

"Emoly Liu <emoly@whamcloud.com>" uploaded a new patch: https://review.whamcloud.com/c/fs/lustre-release/+/68597

It looks like there was still a ZFS OOM in the patched sanityn test_56b after 66 iterations:
https://testing.whamcloud.com/test_sets/0d5b69fc-f289-4ba0-a9f4-e3f882f9b268

Another option is to add "always_except LU-20276 56b" to sanityn to avoid the crashes. That doesn't solve the ZFS allocation issue, and we can hope that this issue is less frequent on servers with more memory.

The regular failure rate is 9/368 ~= 1/40 for test_70b in the past week, and the custom test session crashed after 66 iterations. Not much better, even if it makes a difference. What is strange is that test_71c is an ldiskfs-only test case and is skipped most of the time unless it crashes, so it appears to be purely a timing issue rather than something which is done as part of that subtest.

The OOM being caused by the previous large file free is very helpful.  There was work done in https://github.com/openzfs/zfs/pull/16722  to improve this, those changes are in the 2.4.x releases but they're not a complete fix.  Although, if you read the top comment of the PR there's a good explanation of what the memory consumers are and why.  Anyway, clearly that change is insufficient for the test VMs.

There are a few potentially easy workarounds I'd suggest trying first.

1. Add a "zpool wait -t free" to the large file freeing test case on the OSS.  At a minimum adding it to the end of the test will make sure any background freeing has completed before moving on the to the next test.  If the OOM is happening earlier, that of course won't help.

2. ZFS used to more aggressively throttle the frees, but that limit has been periodically relaxed in the name of performance (see https://github.com/openzfs/zfs/pull/10000 and https://github.com/openzfs/zfs/pull/13938).  The 10000 PR is old enough it wouldn't explain why you're seeing this now, introduced in the zfs-2.0 release, but the 13938 PR change first appears as of the zfs-2.2 release and maybe lines up a bit better.  It may be interesting to try setting "zfs_per_txg_dirty_frees_percent " back to it's previous default of 5 (it was increased to 30).  That will help throttle the frees.  To set it "echo 5 >/sys/module/zfs/parameters/zfs_per_txg_dirty_frees_percent".

3. If that isn't sufficient it may be because the blocks are being freed by a single "dmu_tx_hold_free".  Today there's no mechanism to throttle at a granularity less than a single hold, so if it's done with a single call you can go past the limit.  Breaking this up in to multiple holds in the OSD should allow the throttle to behave better and limit the memory usage if neither 1) of 2) above are sufficient.
